catalog_quote: Lexical tone is present throughout the Nouchi lexicon, no matter the language of origin of each given lexical item; all Nouchi lexical items, regardless of origin of the word, are marked with consistent lexical tone. Certain otherwise identical words are differentiated by their tonal patterns. For example, [dába] ‘to hit,’ is differentiated from [dāba] ‘to eat’ only by differing tonal patterns. The chart in (15) shows that Nouchi lexical items with varying originals are all pronounces with consistent lexical tone. [...] The data in (15) show that Nouchi makes use of lexical tone. Certain otherwise identical words are differentiated by their tonal patterns. For example, [dába] 'to hit,' is differentiated from [dāba] 'to eat' only by differing tonal patterns. new_statements.rule_in_words: Sande analyses Nouchi as having lexical tone on every word (including French-derived and monosyllabic items) plus grammatical tone (all-Low verb melody = past imperfective); she makes no statement about word stress. The competing view (Boutin & Kouadio N'Guessan 2015, HAL p.11) is that Nouchi has no prosodic system of its own but shares that of Ivorian popular French, for which Boutin & Turcsan 2009 (§4.4.7-4.4.8) report word-based rather than phrase-final accentuation that 'ne porte pas toujours sur la dernière syllabe du syntagme ou du mot', an initial accent including on clitics, and sporadic lexical high tones.
new_statements.exceptions: Sande: surface tone of infinitive -e varies, no claim of underlying tone. Ahua 2007/2008 describe 'accentuation' of syllables only as emphatic lengthening marking degree/intensity, not lexical prominence. Boutin & Turcsan (Ivorian French): numerals and 'un' accented; ordinals and acronyms accented on first syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Sande's data are elicited words/short clauses from Abidjan speakers (fieldwork 2012-13); tone claimed at word level. Boutin & Turcsan's accent remarks concern Ivorian French conversational/reading corpus (PFC-CIA), phrase vs word domain explicitly discussed (Ivorian French 'identifies the phonological word with the grammatical word'). Whether Nouchi has a distinct prosodic system from Ivorian French is itself disputed between Sande and Boutin.
new_statements.identity_note: Nouchi (nouc1234) is the Abidjan urban youth language on a français populaire ivoirien base with Dioula/Baoulé/Bété/English lexicon. Sande 2015 treats it as a distinct language with its own tone system; Boutin & Kouadio N'Guessan 2015 argue it is prosodically identical to Ivorian popular French (no separate glottocode; Ivorian French is subsumed under stan1290 French in Glottolog), so the only accent-placement remarks available (Boutin & Turcsan 2009) describe Ivorian French, not Nouchi as such.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Vowel/consonant inventories of Ivorian French and Nouchi; says inclusion of tones in Ivorian French then Nouchi is the most salient hybridisation trait; emphatic high/extra-high tone and vowel lengthening on ideophones/gradable words. No word-stress placement statement.

sources.citation: Boutin, Béatrice Akissi & Jérémie Kouadio N'Guessan. 2015. Le nouchi c'est notre créole en quelque sorte, qui est parlé par presque toute la Côte d'Ivoire. In Peter Blumenthal (ed.), Dynamique des français africains: entre le culturel et le linguistique. Frankfurt: Peter Lang. (HAL author version hal-01408710)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Disputes Sande's claim of a Nouchi-specific tonal system; says Nouchi and français populaire ivoirien have 'le même système phonologique et prosodique' (HAL p.11), and that tones, word-based rather than phrase-based accentuation, and reduction of unstressed syllables were already documented for Ivorian French; quotes Boutin & Turcsan 2009:149 that accent 'ne porte pas toujours sur la dernière syllabe du syntagme ou du mot'.

sources.citation: Boutin, Béatrice Akissi & Gabor Turcsan. 2009. La prononciation du français en Afrique: la Côte d'Ivoire. In J. Durand, B. Laks & C. Lyche (eds), Phonologie, variation et accents du français, 131-152. Paris: Hermès. (HAL author version hal-01411661)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: On Ivorian French (PFC-Abidjan), §4.4.7 'Remarques sur la prosodie': accentuation separates words rather than rhythmic groups and does not always fall on the last syllable of the phrase or word; numerals/un are accented, ordinals and acronyms accented on their first syllable; §4.4.8 mentions 'l'accent initial, y compris celui des clitiques'; some homophones distinguished by a high tone. Not a Nouchi-specific description.

sources.note: §2.3 'Accentuation sur les syllabes des mots': speaker 'accentuation' of syllables serves as a degree marker as in African languages (emphatic lengthening), plus final aspiration; conclusion says Nouchi intonation/prosody still needs a dedicated study. No word-stress position.
